claim_checks.claim: Artifact: an iptables NAT rule and the nftables rule it really became (lab, iptables v1.8.10, Linux 6.17.8, 2026-11-04)
claim_checks.page_says: not checked: cites only the local lab artifact [^4]

claim_checks.claim: Netfilter hooks — its job: call registered functions at fixed points of the packet path, via prerouting, input, forward, output, postrouting (plus per-interface ingress/egress)
claim_checks.page_says: Unlike the other netfilter hooks, the ingress hook is attached to a particular network interface.
claim_checks.note: The five hooks, ingress and egress are all on the page, and ingress is stated to be per-interface. The page never says egress is attached to an interface (it only lists egress in the netdev family row, 1.0.1 / 5.16); the claim widens the per-interface property from ingress to egress.

claim_checks.claim: Connection tracking — its job: record each flow and its state, via hooks at priority −200 in prerouting and output, confirmed last in input and postrouting
claim_checks.page_says: Connection tracking processes run early in prerouting and output hooks to associate packets with tracked connections. … Connection tracking adds new tracked connections at final step in input & postrouting hooks.
claim_checks.note: Priority −200 (NF_IP_PRI_CONNTRACK) in prerouting/output and INT_MAX confirm in input/postrouting both match.

claim_checks.claim: Rule engine (nftables or iptables) — its job: match packets and apply verdicts (accept, drop) or NAT, via chains attached to hooks at priorities (dstnat −100, filter 0, srcnat 100)
claim_checks.page_says: Note that the same keyword maps to different numerical priorities in the bridge family vs. the other families.
claim_checks.note: The values −100/0/100 are on rows labelled 'inet, ip, ip6'; the bridge family maps dstnat to −300, filter to −200 and srcnat to 300. The claim gives the keyword values with no family qualifier.

claim_checks.claim: Hook order per packet type: arriving for this host ingress → prerouting → input; forwarded ingress → prerouting → forward → postrouting; generated locally output → postrouting
claim_checks.page_says: Such forwarded packets follow the path: prerouting, forward and postrouting. … traffic that is generated by local processes follows the output and postrouting path.
claim_checks.note: Input path 'sees the prerouting and input hooks'; ingress takes effect 'even before prerouting'. All three rows match.

claim_checks.claim: Hook entry: each registered chain runs in priority order: raw (−300) before conntrack (−200), mangle (−150), dstnat (−100), filter (0), srcnat (100)
claim_checks.page_says: Within a given hook, Netfilter performs operations in order of increasing numerical priority.
claim_checks.note: Order and values match the rows labelled 'inet, ip, ip6', but the page warns that the same keywords map to other numbers in the bridge family (dstnat −300, filter −200, srcnat 300). The family qualifier is dropped.

claim_checks.claim: NAT chains must use a priority above −200 so conntrack has already run
claim_checks.page_says: NOTE: nat type chains must use priority > -200, which is used by conntrack hooks.

claim_checks.claim: Conntrack: the first packet of a flow creates an entry; later packets match it. The entry is confirmed at the very end of input/postrouting (priority INT_MAX)
claim_checks.page_says: INT_MAX   | NF_IP_PRI_CONNTRACK_CONFIRM   | Connection tracking adds new tracked connections at final step in input & postrouting hooks.
claim_checks.note: Later packets are associated with tracked connections at −200; new connections are added at INT_MAX in input and postrouting.

claim_checks.claim: DNAT (prerouting, dstnat): rewrites the destination before routing, so the routing decision sees the new address (that is why it must be in prerouting)
claim_checks.page_says: PREROUTING (for altering packets as soon as they come in)
claim_checks.note: iptables(8) has no DNAT text (searched 'DNAT'); it does not say the routing decision sees the rewritten address, nor that DNAT must be in PREROUTING. The uncited [^6] says DNAT is valid in PREROUTING and OUTPUT, so 'must be in prerouting' is also contradicted by a cached Rank 1 page (see conflicts).

claim_checks.claim: SNAT / MASQUERADE (postrouting, srcnat): rewrites the source as the packet leaves; MASQUERADE uses the outgoing interface's current address
claim_checks.page_says: Masquerading is equivalent to specifying a mapping to the IP address of the interface the packet is going out … POSTROUTING (for altering packets as they are about to go out)
claim_checks.note: SNAT modifies the source address [^6]; POSTROUTING alters packets about to go out [^5]; MASQUERADE maps to the outgoing interface's address and is meant for dynamically assigned IPs [^6], which covers 'current'.

claim_checks.claim: Replies: conntrack recognizes the reply direction and reverses the translation without consulting NAT rules again — SNAT/DNAT apply to "all future packets in this connection"
claim_checks.page_says: the destination address of the packet should be modified (and all future packets in this connection will also be mangled), and rules should cease being examined.
claim_checks.note: The quoted part and the existence of a REPLY direction (--ctdir) are on the page. That replies get the reverse translation is not stated (searched 'reply', 'reverse'), and 'rules should cease being examined' is about the current packet. 'Without consulting NAT rules again' is true per the uncited [^5] ('consulted when a packet that creates a new connection is encountered'), not per [^6].

claim_checks.claim: iptables vs nftables: iptables uses fixed tables (filter, nat, mangle, raw) with built-in chains; nftables lets you create tables and chains and attach them to hooks with explicit type … hook … priority
claim_checks.page_says: In a major change from iptables, which predefines chains at every hook (i.e. INPUT chain in filter table), nftables predefines no chains at all.
claim_checks.note: Predefined iptables chains vs explicit nftables base chains with a chain type, hook and priority is supported. The iptables table names nat and mangle are not on the page as tables (only raw, filter and security tables are named), and nothing says nftables lets you create tables. The table list is in the uncited [^5] (which names five tables, including security); table creation syntax is in the uncited Quick reference page.

violations.evidence: C9: iptables(8) [^5] has no DNAT text and does not say the routing decision sees the new address or that DNAT must be in PREROUTING.

C9 states 'must be in prerouting' as fact in role 3; the cached Rank 1 [^6] says DNAT is valid in the PREROUTING and OUTPUT chains. The lower rank number does not govern the claim (the doc's own Takeaways and Edge cases also use DNAT in output).
C11: [^6] says SNAT/DNAT mangle 'all future packets in this connection' but not that replies get the reverse translation; 'without consulting NAT rules again' is only in the uncited [^5].
C12: [^1] does not name nat or mangle as iptables tables and does not say nftables lets you create tables; those facts are in the uncited [^5] and Quick reference page.
C2: [^1] says only the ingress hook is attached to a particular interface; the claim extends that to egress.
C4: priorities dstnat −100, filter 0, srcnat 100 are the inet/ip/ip6 values; [^1] notes the bridge family maps the same keywords to other numbers. Qualifier dropped.
C6: same dropped family qualifier for the full priority list raw −300 … srcnat 100.
C18: the saved text of [^7] stops at source line 1000 and lacks the 'table full, dropping packet' warning the References entry says it backs.

Only the rules and the MASQUERADE counter are a captured lab run, and that counter comes from a ping, not the DNAT flow; the 203.0.113.7 → 198.51.100.10:8080 trace is an illustrative table with documentation addresses and no captured output (no conntrack or packet capture).
